content: Knismesis and gargalesis are the scientific terms introduced in 1897 by psychologists G. Stanley Hall and Arthur Allin to describe two distinct types of tickling. Knismesis refers to a light, feather-like tickling sensation. This type of tickling typically does not provoke laughter and is often accompanied by an itching sensation. The phenomenon of knismesis is triggered by low levels of stimulation applied to sensitive areas of the body. It can be induced by a light touch or even a mild electrical current. Additionally, knismesis can be caused by crawling insects or parasites, which prompts scratching or rubbing of the affected area to remove the irritant. This response may have an evolutionary function, as it is observed in many different animal species. For example, it is possible to tickle the area just beneath the snout of a great white shark, which can induce a near-hypnotic trance-like state in the animal. Gargalesis, on the other hand, refers to a more intense form of tickling that induces laughter. This type of tickling involves the repeated application of firm pressure to sensitive areas of the body. Often referred to as heavy tickling, gargalesis is commonly associated with play and laughter. This type of tickling is effective in humans and primates and may also occur in other species. The nerves responsible for transmitting sensations of light touch and itch differ from those that transmit sensations of firm touch, pressure, and vibration. This distinction may explain the differences in the sensations produced by knismesis and gargalesis. The relative proportions of itch versus touch sensations likely contribute to the contrasting experiences of these two types of tickling. While it is possible to induce a knismesis response in oneself, it is generally impossible to produce the gargalesis response, also known as gargalesthesia, on oneself.
